title: Canada Doubles Low-Wage Work Permit Duration to Two Years for New LMIAs
excerpt: Low-wage LMIA applications filed on or after November 6 can support up to two years of employment, lengthening the TFWP permits IRCC can issue — but existing permits are not extended automatically.
body:
• Low-wage Labour Market Impact Assessments (LMIAs) submitted on or after November 6, 2026 can now support employment for up to two years, double the previous one-year maximum — and the LMIA's duration caps the work permit IRCC can issue.
  • Existing permits are not extended automatically: to stay longer, a worker's employer must obtain a new LMIA and the worker must apply to extend.
  • Early childhood educators joined the occupations exempt from the refusal-to-process rule in metro areas with unemployment of 6% or higher; that moratorium still covers 30 metro areas including Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal.
  • A bigger, occupation-based overhaul proposed for March 1, 2027 depends on provinces and territories opting in — it is not yet in force.

Canada has doubled the maximum employment duration supported by low-wage Labour Market Impact Assessments, from one year to two, in changes to the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TFWP) that took effect on November 6, 2026. Because the LMIA's duration sets the maximum length of the work permit Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) can issue, the change directly lengthens the permits available to workers hired through the program's low-wage stream.

Who is affected — exactly

The change covers employers and workers in the TFWP's low-wage stream: positions paying less than 120% of the median hourly wage in the province or territory where the job is located. CIC News put the current low-wage threshold at $36.92 an hour in Ontario and $38.40 in British Columbia. It applies only to LMIA applications submitted on or after November 6, 2026. It does not change the high-wage stream, and it does not, by itself, give anyone a work permit: an employer still needs a positive or neutral LMIA — ESDC's finding that no qualified Canadian citizen or permanent resident was available — and the worker must still qualify for the permit from IRCC.

What changed, precisely

Before November 6, a low-wage LMIA could support at most one year of employment, so employers who wanted to keep a worker had to apply again. An LMIA submitted now can request up to two years, according to Employment and Social Development Canada's November 6 announcement. "While Canadians must always be first in line for available jobs, employers in key sectors continue to face labour shortages that can limit growth and affect communities across the country," said Jobs and Families Minister Patty Hajdu.

"A well-managed immigration system must be predictable, sustainable and responsive to Canada's economic needs."

— Lena Metlege Diab, Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship

The high-unemployment moratorium still applies

The longer duration does not lift the separate restriction that has stopped many low-wage applications since September 2024: ESDC will not process low-wage LMIAs for non-exempt jobs in Census Metropolitan Areas (CMAs) where unemployment is 6% or higher. CIC News counts 30 affected CMAs, including Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal, Calgary, Edmonton and Halifax, and ESDC updates the list quarterly — the next update is scheduled for January 8, 2027. Exempt sectors already included healthcare, construction, agriculture and food processing. From November 6, early childhood educators are exempt as well, a change aimed at childcare shortages.

What to do next

If you hold a low-wage TFWP permit now, nothing about your permit changes on its own. To extend it, your employer must first obtain a new LMIA — and an application filed now can support up to two years. Apply to extend before your current permit expires to keep maintained status, which lets you keep working under the old permit's conditions until IRCC decides. If your permit expires in two weeks or less and the LMIA decision is still pending, concurrent processing may apply; IRCC eliminated the time limit on concurrent processing on October 28, 2026. The program rules are set out on CIC News' explainer and ESDC's announcement above.

What is proposed for 2027 — not yet law

ESDC has also proposed a more regional system from March 1, 2027, contingent on provinces and territories opting in. In large metro areas with unemployment below 6%, low-wage access would be limited to occupations on the Canadian Occupational Projection System shortage list plus occupations provinces add or remove. Rural communities would keep access to all occupations. Provinces could also ask to raise the low-wage workforce cap for employers in selected communities from 10% to 15%; priority sectors would keep their existing 20% limit. Budget 2026 backs the program with $151.5 million over five years for service delivery and $82 million over four years for the Migrant Worker Support Program. None of the 2027 measures applies today — employers should plan on the rules now in force and watch whether their province opts in.
